Aji: Latent potential in a position — stones or sequences that aren't active now but could become useful or threatening later.
Atari: A threat to capture: a group has only one liberty remaining and will be captured on the next move unless it escapes or captures first.
Boshi: A capping move placed directly above an opponent's stone, preventing it from extending toward the center and limiting its development.
Clamp: A tesuji where a stone is placed between two opponent stones of the same color, forcing them apart or creating cutting threats.
Dame: A neutral point adjacent to both players' territory, or a liberty of no strategic value. Often filled at the end of the game.
Dan: The rank system for strong players above kyu: 1 dan (amateur) is strong, up to 9 dan (professional). Higher is stronger.
Double Ko: A position with two simultaneous ko fights. Under normal ko rules, the player who first has to yield one ko loses the other.
Empty Triangle: An inefficient shape where three stones of the same color form a triangle with an empty space at the middle, wasting one stone's potential.
Endgame: The final phase of the game (yose) where both sides secure territory and fill neutral points. Precision here often determines the winner.
Fuseki: The opening phase of a game on a full 19×19 board, before contact fighting begins. Strategy focuses on balance, framework, and direction.
Geta: A net — a technique to capture a stone by surrounding it so it cannot escape in any direction, even though it isn't yet enclosed.
Gote: A move that does not require an immediate response; the player playing gote loses the initiative (sente) to the opponent.
Hamete: A trick play or trap that appears locally clever but is unsound against correct response. Often used to lure inexperienced players.
Hane: A move that goes around the end of an opponent's line of stones, bending past their edge.
Hasami: A pincer — a move that attacks an opponent's newly played stone by flanking it, preventing it from settling easily.
Influence: Outward-facing power projected toward the center or open areas by a thick group, often more valuable than immediate territory.
Joseki: Established locally optimal sequences in the corner or along the edge, considered fair for both sides when played correctly.
Keima: A knight's move — a diagonal jump one step in one direction and two steps in another, like a chess knight. Used for quick development.
Ko: A rule preventing immediate repetition of a board position. A single-stone capture that could be immediately recaptured must be delayed by playing elsewhere first.
Komi: Points given to White to compensate for Black playing first. Standard komi on 19×19 is 6.5 or 7.5 points.
Kosumi: A diagonal move: placing a stone diagonally adjacent to one of your own stones, typically to strengthen a corner or reduce liberties.
Kyu: Rank below dan. 30 kyu is a complete beginner; 1 kyu is just below amateur dan level. Lower number = stronger.
Ladder: A capture sequence (shicho) in which the attacker chases a stone in a zigzag pattern toward the edge of the board.
Liberty: An empty intersection directly adjacent (not diagonal) to a stone or group. A group with zero liberties is captured.
Moyo: A large framework or potential territory — an area loosely surrounded by a player's stones that may become actual territory if defended.
Net: See Geta — surrounding a stone so it cannot escape even without directly enclosing it.
Nobi: A solid extension — extending directly along a line by one step, often used to strengthen a group or connect stones.
Oba: A large-scale urgent point in the opening or middle game that both players want to occupy — a "big point".
Peep: Playing at a cutting point inside an opponent's shape to threaten to cut it apart, forcing a response.
Ponnuki: The shape formed when four stones capture a single stone at the center. Considered a very efficient, powerful shape.
Sagari: A descent — a move that drops down from a higher position to the edge or to a lower line, typically to secure territory or life.
Seki: Mutual life — a position where neither player can capture the other without being captured first. Neither group is alive in the normal sense.
Sente: Having the initiative: your move requires a response, so you retain the right to play next in another area.
Shimari: A corner enclosure — two stones of the same color that together secure a corner and prevent easy invasion.
Snapback: A tesuji: after the opponent captures a stone, the resulting shape allows an immediate recapture of a larger group.
Squeeze: A tesuji that reduces an opponent's liberties by playing inside their space, forcing them to capture and creating a ladder or net.
Suji: Sound technique — a well-reasoned, structurally correct move as opposed to a crude or inefficient one.
Tengen: The center point of the board (the 10-10 point on a 19×19). Occasionally played as an opening move for influence.
Tenuki: Ignoring a local threat and playing elsewhere — a strategically bold move that says the global board position is more urgent.
Tesuji: A clever tactical move that solves a local problem efficiently — often unexpected, exploiting a weakness in the opponent's shape.
Thickness: A group that has no weaknesses and projects strong influence outward. Thick groups are not necessarily territory but are powerful.
Tsumego: A life-and-death problem: a puzzle where you must determine whether a group can live or be killed, and find the correct move.
Vital Point: The single most important point in a local position — often the point that, if occupied, either gives life or kills a group.
Zankai: After a large-scale battle ends, residual threats or aji left in the settled area that may be activated later.
